Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-25
Start: 15:00 PDT

Attendees: Alyssa (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Anna (CTO), Tom (Lead ML Eng), Priya (Infra), Kevin (PM)

Topics: TTFT, streaming, sequence length distribution, kernel selection, KV cache/retention, quantization, dedicated vs hosted routing, SLA impact

[00:00] Alyssa: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, quick check-in for the latency tuning POC. Marcus and I will go over the latest runs and then open Qs.
[00:15] Anna: yep thanks, we ran the overnight benchmark, saw TTFT around 220ms for the 512 seq baseline, p50-ish, but p99 was spiking to 1.6s which is worrying.
[00:27] Marcus: okay, that matches what we saw; the streaming path helped reduce TTFT for shorter outputs but for longer sequences the kernel fallback and attention windows kicked in. note: some of the telemetry mislabeled kernels as "opt-k" in the run, so ignore that label.
[00:45] Tom: can you remind me what exact model config you had — model size, quant, gpu type? we were trying the 13B fp16 with q4 for evaluation on a V100 equivalent?
[01:02] Marcus: sure — in staging we used an A40-equivalent, model is 13B, we tried both fp16 and q4_0 quant profiles; batch size 1 for latency, and streaming enabled. For the long sequences the runtime selected a different kernel path (attention tiling changed) which increased per-token cost and latency.
[01:22] Priya: small note — our production infra is GCP A2s (A100), so numbers will differ; I'll share the exact cpu/gpu trace.
[01:31] Kevin: what's TTFT exactly here? first token time, right, not first byte?
[01:35] Marcus: yeah TTFT time to first token from request accept, includes prefill and initial attention pass. streaming reduces the time by starting output before full decode, but it's sensitive to model chunking.
[01:50] Anna: streaming sounded promising, but we saw tokenization variance and sometimes the first token is delayed because of long prefix prompts (we sent 1.2k tokens in some tests).
[02:05] Marcus: right, sequence length distribution matters — if you have heavy long-context prompts, caching prefixes (KV cache) helps a lot but you need sticky routing so requests hit the same instance with the warm KV cache.
[02:18] Tom: do you support sticky session routing on dedicated? we need to keep rate-latency predictable for our fraud model.
[02:24] Alyssa: yes, for Dedicated we can do instance pinning or session routing; for Hosted we offer best-effort KV cache but not guaranteed sticky unless you pick a reserved pool.
[02:36] Priya: security question — are KV cache contents persisted to disk? we need to ensure no PII leakage and KMS encryption at rest.
[02:44] Marcus: no, KV cache is in-memory only for the serving runtime; persisted checkpoints for warm starts are optional and encrypted with customer KMS in Private deployments. We'll include the doc link after the call.
[02:58] Anna: great. back to latency — can you walk through what you changed since last week that moved the TTFT from ~350ms down to ~220ms for small prompts?
[03:09] Marcus: two big changes: first, we enabled streaming with adaptive chunking so the runtime emits the first token earlier; second, we tuned kernel selection heuristics to favor smaller prefill kernels on short prefixes — that avoids an expensive full attention kernel. Also we changed scheduler to prioritize single-request low-latency over batching for this pilot.
[03:34] Tom: but that scheduler change increases unit cost right? we saw cost go up by ~8%.
[03:39] Alyssa: yes there's a tradeoff — lower TTFT usually increases tokens/sec efficiency; we can propose hybrid configs: low-latency mode during business hours and batched/cheaper mode off-peak.
[03:51] Kevin: can you show the p50/p95/p99 numbers for both modes?
[03:55] Marcus: quick readout from today's run: low-latency mode p50=220ms, p95=430ms, p99=1.6s. batched mode p50=420ms, p95=650ms, p99=900ms but cost per token down ~25%.
[04:13] Anna: p99 1.6s is borderline for us; our SLA target is 1s at p99 for the fraud check pipeline.
[04:21] Marcus: understood — two knobs to try: 1) kernel sweep to find a kernel variant that keeps p99 lower for long sequences, 2) improve prefix caching hit rate by sticky routing and adjusting KV retention TTL.
[04:33] Tom: how long does a kernel sweep take? we need results by next Wednesday.
[04:38] Marcus: we can run an automated sweep across quant profiles (fp16, q4, q8-int) and kernel variants — a full sweep across all combos with our infra takes ~24-48h, but we can prioritize the most promising subset and have initial data in 48h.
[04:52] Priya: please prioritize A100-equivalent runs since that's our target hardware.
[04:56] Marcus: noted. we'll pin the runner to A100 pool.
[05:01] Anna: on quantization — we saw quality degradation at q8 and some tokenization artifacts at q4_0 in a few transcripts. are you seeing that too?
[05:09] Marcus: yes q8 introduced garbling on some rare tokens; q4_0 was mostly fine but had a slight bump in hallucination rate on long contexts. we'll include evals across your prompt set.
[05:21] Kevin: is there an easy way to test streaming + function calls? our pipeline uses tool-calling heavily.
[05:27] Marcus: function/tool-calling with streaming is supported, but you need to instrument your client to commit the function call as soon as the signature is emitted. That can add friction; we'll share a sample snippet.
[05:38] Tom: one more infra question — what about kernel fallback during OOMs? last run showed a fallback to a slower kernel and that spiked p99.
[05:47] Marcus: fallback happens if the preferred kernel runs out of memory; we can configure memory margins and pre-select kernels for your max seq length to avoid fallback. also quantized kernels have smaller memory footprint so fewer fallbacks.
[06:02] Anna: ok action items?
[06:05] Alyssa: quick recap — Marcus will run the kernel/quant sweep on A100, Priya will send traces, Tom will validate KV cache behavior, and I'll send pricing + SOC2 link. We'll reconvene after initial sweep results.
[06:20] Kevin: can we also get a short doc explaining tradeoffs: TTFT vs cost vs p99 and recommended configs per workload?
[06:27] Alyssa: yes we'll draft a one-pager.
[06:30] (overlap) Tom: also want to consider dedicated reserved pool if p99 doesn't stabilize on hosted.
[06:36] Marcus: we can model cost difference and expected p99 gains for Dedicated — typically sticky routing + reserved instances reduce p99 spikes by improving cache hit rate.
[06:47] Anna: thanks all, this was productive.
[06:50] Alyssa: thanks — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule the benchmark next Tuesday at 10am PT.
[06:58] End of recording.
